title: Eat, my coat
hookLine: turned away in rags, welcomed in a fur coat, he spoons the soup into his sleeve
last: LOOKING UNDER THE LAMP — SEARCH WHERE YOU LOST IT.

lines: A BANQUET IN HIS OWN TOWN.
cards: Walk into a nice restaurant in sweatpants. Now walk in dressed up. Watch how the host looks at you, where they seat you, how fast the water arrives.
Most of us have been on both sides of that look, and most of us have given it too, without meaning to. Nasruddin, the wise fool, got that look once, at a banquet in his own town.
His answer became a proverb in Turkish, said to this day whenever someone is treated by their clothes and not by who they are.

teach.b: The story usually goes like this. There's a feast, and Nasruddin is invited. He comes straight from work in his everyday clothes, worn and dusty.
Nobody greets him or finds him a seat. The dishes go around and somehow skip him. So he slips home and puts on his finest clothes: a big, beautiful fur coat.
He walks back in, and everything changes. The host rushes over: welcome, welcome!

teach.h: A FUR COAT: THE BEST SOUP.
teach.b: He's seated near the top of the table, the best soup set in front of him.
And Nasruddin dips the sleeve of his fur coat into the bowl and says: eat, my coat, eat! The guests stare. Mulla, what are you doing?
Well, he says, it was the coat you welcomed. It seems only fair the coat should eat. In Turkish, eat, my coat, eat is a saying people still use, a whole sermon in three words.
The old traditions knew this problem well.
In Nasruddin's own Muslim world, a well-known saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, teaches that God does not look at your appearance or your wealth, but at your heart and your deeds.
And a letter in the New Testament, from James, describes almost the same scene: a rich man in fine clothes is shown to the best seat, and a poor man in shabby clothes is told to stand at the back.
Different homes, same banquet: the coat gets the soup, and the person goes hungry. Nasruddin doesn't lecture anyone. He just feeds the coat, and lets the whole room see what they've been doing.

how: In Turkey the saying "eat, my coat, eat" is still used to call out treatment based on appearances; many traditions teach hospitality that welcomes every guest the same, such as the Sikh langar and the Muslim and Jewish duty to honor the guest.

games.q: you're Nasruddin. you've come back in a fur coat, and now you're seated near the top with the best soup in front of you. what do you do?
o: eat it, and enjoy the evening.
dip your coat's sleeve in the soup and tell it to eat.
games.why: "eat, my coat, eat!" it was the coat they welcomed, so it seems only fair the coat should eat.

practice: Honestly, and without beating yourself up, think back over the last few days: was there someone you treated a little better, or a little worse, because of how they looked, what they wore, what they drove?
The cashier, the new coworker, the person asking for change. Picture that person without the coat: just a person, hungry for the same things you are.

wordCard.voice: Eat. Nasruddin's words to his fur coat: eat, my coat, eat, because the coat was welcomed, and the man was not.

orig.note: Turkish: eat, my fur coat, eat. Nasreddin Hoca's line, still used as a saying about being judged by appearances.

carryVoice: Your line: feed the person. The coat never needed the soup; the person did. Day thirty-seven.
